title: Molality, Mole Fraction and Parts per Million
short: Other ways to state concentration, each suited to a different job.
trouble: Students divide by liters of solution, or by the mass of the whole solution, for molality instead of by kilograms of solvent.

blocks.html: Molarity counts moles of solute per liter of solution. It is easy to measure out, but its volume changes a little with temperature, and it is not the natural unit for every job. Three other units fill the gaps.

Molality, $m = \dfrac{\text{mol solute}}{\text{kg solvent}}$ (unit mol/kg). Mole fraction, $\chi_A = \dfrac{\text{mol A}}{\text{total mol}}$ (no unit; all the fractions add to 1). Mass percent $= \dfrac{\text{mass solute}}{\text{mass solution}} \times 100$. Parts per million, ppm $= \dfrac{\text{mass solute}}{\text{mass solution}} \times 10^{6}$ (for dilute water solutions, 1 ppm is about 1 mg per liter).

Each unit suits a job. Molality uses masses, which don't change when the solution warms or cools, so it is the unit for freezing and boiling points. Mole fraction counts particles of every kind, which is what decides a vapor pressure or a partial pressure. Mass percent is what you get by weighing. Parts per million keeps tiny amounts readable: "0.0002% lead" becomes "2 ppm". Note what each one divides by: molality by the solvent alone, in kilograms; mass percent and ppm by the whole solution.

blocks.cap: One salt solution, four ways: molarity, molality, mole fraction and mass percent.

blocks.title: Molality
blocks.q: $10.0\ \text{g}$ of NaCl ($58.44\ \text{g/mol}$) is dissolved in $250.0\ \text{g}$ of water. Find the molality.
steps: Kilograms of solvent: $250.0\ \text{g} = 0.2500\ \text{kg}$ (the water only, not the water plus the salt).

blocks.title: Mole fraction
blocks.q: A solution contains $46.08\ \text{g}$ of ethanol ($46.08\ \text{g/mol}$) and $90.10\ \text{g}$ of water ($18.02\ \text{g/mol}$). Find the mole fraction of ethanol.

blocks.title: Parts per million
blocks.q: A $500.0\ \text{g}$ water sample contains $1.2\ \text{mg}$ of dissolved iron. Express the iron concentration in ppm.

blocks.html: For a dilute water solution, a liter of solution is very nearly a kilogram of water, so molarity and molality are almost equal there. They differ more and more as the solution gets concentrated, which the next topic works out with densities.

For molality, dividing by liters of solution (that is molarity) or by the mass of the whole solution. Molality's denominator is the mass of the solvent only, in kilograms. Check: write the units out, mol/kg of solvent, and make sure the number under the bar excludes the solute's mass.
